tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The neighbour who waters our plants is away this week.
The recipe which my aunt shared it needs less salt.
The library who opens on Sundays stays busy all day.
The bus that stops outside the school leaves at eight.
The park, that was closed after the storm, reopens tomorrow.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The neighbour who waters our plants is away this week.**

In a defining relative clause, "who" correctly points to a person and identifies which neighbour we mean. The clause is essential information, so there are no commas around it. Nothing else tries to occupy the subject slot of "waters," so the structure is clean.

So the statement holds: restrictive "who" correctly identifies the neighbour.

**B) The recipe which my aunt shared it needs less salt.**

The relative "which" already stands for the recipe as the object of "shared," so leftover "it" fills the same slot twice. English allows only one object filler here. Drop the pronoun to leave a single, clear object relative.

**Trap:** Residual "it" after an object relative is a classic exam near-miss that still looks almost grammatical.

So the statement is false: repair to "The recipe which my aunt shared needs less salt."

**C) The library who opens on Sundays stays busy all day.**

A library is a thing or place, not a person, so "who" is the wrong relative pronoun. Defining clauses about institutions use "which" or "that." Reserve "who" for human heads.

So the statement is false: repair to "The library which/that opens on Sundays stays busy all day."

**D) The bus that stops outside the school leaves at eight.**

Restrictive "that" correctly defines which bus leaves at eight. The clause is essential to identify the bus, so no commas appear. The relative is the subject of "stops," and the sentence reads cleanly.

So the statement holds: defining "that" correctly picks out the bus.

**E) The park, that was closed after the storm, reopens tomorrow.**

Commas mark a non-restrictive clause that adds extra detail about a known park. In careful exam English, that extra information after commas needs "which," not "that." Swap the pronoun and keep the commas.

**Trap:** Comma + "that" for a thing is a frequent exam trap because the commas look correct while the pronoun is not.

So the statement is false: repair to "The park, which was closed after the storm, reopens tomorrow."
tasks.solution_overview:
These five sentences all turn on relative clauses that pick out a neighbour, a recipe, a library, a bus, or a park.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Ask whether the head noun is a person or a thing, and whether commas mark the clause as extra information. Also check that the relative pronoun itself fills the subject or object slot — no leftover object pronoun such as "it."

**Part 2: How to decide.**

In defining (no-comma) clauses, "who/that" fit people and "which/that" fit things. After commas, use "which" for things, never "that," and never leave a second object after the relative. Mark each sentence true only when those three checks all clear.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The chef whose soup won the contest teaches on Saturdays.
The cyclist who's helmet cracked bought a new one.
The concert, which sold out in an hour, starts at seven.
The students that organised the bake sale raised enough for the trip.
The garage, who stores our bikes, needs a new lock.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The chef whose soup won the contest teaches on Saturdays.**

"Whose" correctly encodes possession: the soup belongs to the chef. You can rephrase the idea as "the chef's soup," which is exactly what "whose" packs into a relative clause. The defining clause needs no commas.

So the statement holds: "whose" correctly marks the chef's possession.

**B) The cyclist who's helmet cracked bought a new one.**

"Who's" expands only to "who is" or "who has," so "who's helmet" would mean "who is helmet." That reading is nonsense; the sentence needs belonging, not a contraction. Possession after a person head takes "whose."

**Trap:** "Who's" versus "whose" is a high-frequency near-miss because the spellings sound identical.

So the statement is false: repair to "The cyclist whose helmet cracked bought a new one."

**C) The concert, which sold out in an hour, starts at seven.**

The commas signal non-essential information about an already-identified concert. For a thing in that slot, "which" is the right pronoun. The clause adds colour without redefining which concert is meant.

So the statement holds: non-restrictive "which" correctly adds extra detail.

**D) The students that organised the bake sale raised enough for the trip.**

In defining clauses about people, "that" is acceptable for identifying which students organised the sale. The clause is essential, so there are no commas. "Who" would sound a touch more formal, but "that" is not an error.

So the statement holds: restrictive "that" for people is acceptable here.

**E) The garage, who stores our bikes, needs a new lock.**

A garage is a building, not a person, so "who" cannot head the relative. Places and buildings take "which" (especially once commas mark the clause as extra information). Swap the pronoun and keep the non-restrictive commas.

So the statement is false: repair to "The garage, which stores our bikes, needs a new lock."
tasks.solution_overview:
Here the focus shifts to possession, contractions, and the familiar who/which split across a chef, a cyclist, a concert, students, and a garage.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Separate "who's" (who is / who has) from "whose" (belonging). Keep "who" for people and "which" for places, buildings, and events — especially once commas mark a non-restrictive clause.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

If you can rephrase as "X's Y," you almost always want "whose." Expand every "who's" before you tick true. For things with commas, expect "which"; for people in defining clauses, "who" or "that" are both acceptable.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The festival, that locals love, fills the square each July.
The tutor whom we hired last autumn still helps on Fridays.
The kettle which boils too slowly needs replacing.
The friend who we invited yesterday cannot come after all.
The photos that Maya printed them are still on the table.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The festival, that locals love, fills the square each July.**

The commas already show that the relative is extra information about a known festival. After commas, exam English wants "which" for things, never "that." Change only the pronoun; leave the commas in place.

**Trap:** Comma + "that" for a thing looks tidy but fails the non-restrictive pronoun rule.

So the statement is false: repair to "The festival, which locals love, fills the square each July."

**B) The tutor whom we hired last autumn still helps on Fridays.**

Formal "whom" correctly marks the tutor as the object of "hired": we hired the tutor. If you can swap in "him/her," "whom" is the careful choice. The structure is polished exam English as written.

So the statement holds: object "whom" correctly follows "hired."

**C) The kettle which boils too slowly needs replacing.**

Defining "which" correctly restricts which kettle needs replacing. No commas are required because the clause is essential. British formal writing often keeps "which" even in defining clauses about things; "that" would also work.

So the statement holds: restrictive "which" cleanly defines the kettle.

**D) The friend who we invited yesterday cannot come after all.**

We invited the friend, so the relative is an object inside the clause. Bare object "who" (with no preposition before it) is widely accepted in modern usage. Exams may prefer "whom" after a preposition, but here bare "who" is fine.

So the statement holds: object "who" without a preceding preposition is acceptable.

**E) The photos that Maya printed them are still on the table.**

The relative "that" already stands for the photos as the object of "printed." Residual "them" doubles that object and must go. Keep the relative and delete the leftover pronoun.

**Trap:** A second object pronoun after the relative is a reliable automatic fail on exam scripts.

So the statement is false: repair to "The photos that Maya printed are still on the table."
tasks.solution_overview:
This set mixes comma rules, object relatives (who/whom), and another leftover pronoun around a festival, a tutor, a kettle, a friend, and some photos.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Spot commas first — they ban "that" in careful exam English. Then ask whether the relative is the object of the verb inside the clause, and whether any residual "them/it" still sits where the relative already sits.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Non-restrictive → "which" for things. Object of "hired" can be formal "whom"; bare object "who" is usually accepted without a preposition. If the clause already does the object's job, delete any leftover pronoun before you mark true.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The runner who finished first still looked fresh.
The map that we borrowed shows every hiking trail.
The café whose windows face the river stays open late.
The singer who's opening the show arrives at six.
The film which the class watched last week was subtitled.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The runner who finished first still looked fresh.**

Restrictive "who" identifies which runner finished first; the clause is needed, so there are no commas. The relative is the subject of "finished." This is a textbook defining person-clause.

So the statement holds: defining "who" correctly picks out the runner.

**B) The map that we borrowed shows every hiking trail.**

Defining "that" correctly restricts which map we borrowed. Inside the clause the relative is the object of "borrowed," a standard pattern for things. No commas are needed.

So the statement holds: restrictive object "that" is fully grammatical.

**C) The café whose windows face the river stays open late.**

"Whose" can mark possession for things as well as people: the café's windows face the river. Rephrase as "the café's windows" and the belonging reading is exact. The possessive relative is the right tool here.

**Tip:** "Whose + noun" works for inanimate heads in careful English.

So the statement holds: "whose" correctly marks the café's windows.

**D) The singer who's opening the show arrives at six.**

"Who's" correctly expands to "who is" before the participle "opening." Try the expansion in place — "the singer who is opening the show" — and the line still works. The contraction is therefore justified.

So the statement holds: "who's" equals "who is" and fits the progressive.

**E) The film which the class watched last week was subtitled.**

Restrictive "which" correctly defines the film the class watched. Either "which" or "that" works in defining clauses about things. No commas appear because the clause is essential.

So the statement holds: defining "which" correctly identifies the film.
tasks.solution_overview:
All five sentences are clean models — use them as a reference sheet for people, things, possession, and a genuine contraction.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Confirm defining "who/that/which," possessive "whose" for a café's windows, and "who's" that really expands to "who is." Nothing here is trying to trick you with commas or leftover pronouns.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Ask person vs thing, then ask whether you need belonging or a contraction. If every piece fits — relative, head noun, and role inside the clause — mark true and move on.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The cousin with whom we share a flat cooks on Sundays.
The playlist, that includes every song from the trip, is private.
Anyone who's keys are missing should check lost property.
The museum which we visited last month displays local pottery.
The coach that designed the drills will explain them tonight.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The cousin with whom we share a flat cooks on Sundays.**

Preposition + "whom" is the formal pattern when the cousin is the object of "with": we share a flat with the cousin. Keep the preposition and use "whom" for people. The structure is polished exam English.

So the statement holds: "with whom" correctly marks the cousin after the preposition.

**B) The playlist, that includes every song from the trip, is private.**

Commas mark a non-restrictive clause about a known playlist. That extra information needs "which," not "that," in careful exam English. Swap the pronoun and keep the commas.

**Trap:** Commas + "that" for a thing is a classic exam fail that still looks tidy at a glance.

So the statement is false: repair to "The playlist, which includes every song from the trip, is private."

**C) Anyone who's keys are missing should check lost property.**

Possession requires "whose," not the contraction "who's." Expand "who's keys" to "who is keys" and the error is obvious. Anyone whose keys are missing is the intended belonging reading.

**Trap:** "Who's" before a noun that needs belonging is a high-frequency whose/who's trap.

So the statement is false: repair to "Anyone whose keys are missing should check lost property."

**D) The museum which we visited last month displays local pottery.**

Defining "which" correctly identifies the museum we visited. Object relatives for things can keep "which" or "that," and the clause is essential, so no commas appear. Informal style could even omit the pronoun, but keeping it is fully correct.

So the statement holds: restrictive object "which" cleanly defines the museum.

**E) The coach that designed the drills will explain them tonight.**

Restrictive "that" for a person is acceptable in a defining clause that identifies which coach. "Who" is often preferred for people in careful style, but "that" is not marked wrong here. The clause is essential and needs no commas.

So the statement holds: defining "that" for a person is acceptable.
tasks.solution_overview:
Preposition + whom, commas that ban "that," and another who's/whose swap sit across a cousin, a playlist, keys, a museum, and a coach.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

After a preposition referring to a person, prefer "whom." Commas still forbid "that" for things. Expand every "who's" before you mark possession true — "who is keys" never works.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Scan for a preposition immediately before the relative, then for commas, then for contractions. Defining "which/that" for places and people can stand when the rest of the grammar is clean.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The bakery from which we order bread raised its prices slightly.
The volunteer whom neighbours praised organised the litter pick.
The novel that Sam finished last night it still sits on the shelf.
Brighton, which hosts the festival, fills with visitors in May.
The friends who cake the party brought later left early.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The bakery from which we order bread raised its prices slightly.**

"From which" correctly links a thing after a preposition: we order bread from the bakery. Keeping the preposition with "which" is the formal pattern exams reward. Stranding ("which we order bread from") is more informal.

So the statement holds: "from which" correctly attaches the preposition to the bakery.

**B) The volunteer whom neighbours praised organised the litter pick.**

"Whom" correctly marks the volunteer as the object of "praised": neighbours praised the volunteer. If you can replace the relative with "him/her," "whom" is justified. The defining clause needs no commas.

So the statement holds: object "whom" correctly follows "praised."

**C) The novel that Sam finished last night it still sits on the shelf.**

The relative "that" already stands for the novel as the object of "finished." Residual "it" before "still sits" doubles that object. Delete "it" and leave the relative to do the job alone.

**Trap:** Keeping both the relative and "it" for the same object is a classic residual-pronoun trap.

So the statement is false: repair to "The novel that Sam finished last night still sits on the shelf."

**D) Brighton, which hosts the festival, fills with visitors in May.**

Non-restrictive "which" correctly adds a known fact about Brighton. Named places with commas almost always take "which," not "that," because the city is already identified. The clause is extra information, not a restricted picker.

So the statement holds: commas + "which" correctly gloss the named city.

**E) The friends who cake the party brought later left early.**

Word order inside the relative collapses: "who cake the party brought" is not English. Rebuild the clause as a normal statement after the relative — subject, verb, object. The friends brought the party cake, then later left early.

So the statement is false: repair to "The friends who brought the party cake later left early."
tasks.solution_overview:
Preposition + which, object whom, a residual "it," a city name with commas, and a collapsed word-order clause share the spotlight.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Keep the preposition with "which/whom" in formal answers. Delete leftover object pronouns. Rebuild any relative clause whose internal order has collapsed into nonsense.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Read the relative clause as a mini-statement after the pronoun. If an "it" remains where that mini-statement already has its object, cut it. If word order inside the clause fails, rewrite it as a normal statement and only then judge the whole sentence.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The neighbour to whom the parcel was delivered signed for it.
The suitcase who's zip is broken stays in the loft.
Drivers whose licences have expired must renew them online.
The beach that we walked along at dusk was almost empty.
The headteacher, that announced the trip, answered questions calmly.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The neighbour to whom the parcel was delivered signed for it.**

"To whom" is the formal object pattern after a preposition: the parcel was delivered to the neighbour. Preposition + "whom" is almost always safe for people in exam English. Keep the preposition together with the relative.

So the statement holds: "to whom" correctly marks the neighbour after the preposition.

**B) The suitcase who's zip is broken stays in the loft.**

A suitcase's zip needs belonging, marked with "whose," not the contraction "who's." Expand "who's zip" to "who is zip" and the misfit is immediate. "Whose" works for inanimate heads as well as people.

**Trap:** "Who's" versus "whose" is a near-miss because the spellings sound identical while only "whose" marks belonging.

So the statement is false: repair to "The suitcase whose zip is broken stays in the loft."

**C) Drivers whose licences have expired must renew them online.**

"Whose" correctly marks possession for people in a defining clause: the drivers' licences have expired. The pattern works with plural noun heads just as with singular. No commas are needed because the clause identifies which drivers.

So the statement holds: "whose" correctly marks the drivers' licences.

**D) The beach that we walked along at dusk was almost empty.**

Restrictive "that" correctly defines which beach we walked along. Object "that/which" can often be omitted informally ("The beach we walked along…"), but keeping "that" is fully correct. The clause is essential, so there are no commas.

So the statement holds: defining place-clause "that" is grammatical.

**E) The headteacher, that announced the trip, answered questions calmly.**

Non-restrictive information about a named person needs "who," not "that." Commas already signal that the clause is extra; the pronoun still has to match a human head. Titles and roles with commas follow the same ban on "that."

**Trap:** Commas + person still demand "who"; "that" is a near-miss because defining people-clauses do allow "that."

So the statement is false: repair to "The headteacher, who announced the trip, answered questions calmly."
tasks.solution_overview:
Formal "to whom," possession for things and people, defining "that," and a comma + "that" about a person are the checks in this set.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Preposition + whom is almost always safe for people. "Whose" marks belonging for licence holders and suitcase zips alike. Non-restrictive clauses about people need "who," never "that."

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Expand every "who's" before you mark true. If you see commas around a person's clause, demand "who." Defining object clauses with "that/which" can stand when no leftover pronoun appears.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The email which Jess sent yesterday still needs a reply.
The author of who the novel was written declined the interview.
The bridge that crosses the canal is closed for repairs.
Guests which arrive early may wait in the lobby.
The trainer whose tips improved my serve will join practice.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The email which Jess sent yesterday still needs a reply.**

Defining "which" correctly identifies the email Jess sent. Subject or object relatives both allow "which/that" for things. No commas are needed because the clause is essential.

So the statement holds: restrictive "which" cleanly defines the email.

**B) The author of who the novel was written declined the interview.**

After a preposition referring to a person, use "whom," not "who." "Of who" is almost never correct in careful English. A fully formal repair uses "of whom," though a plainer rephrase of the passive relative is often clearer.

**Trap:** Preposition + person almost always wants "whom," so "of who" is a reliable red flag.

So the statement is false: repair to "The author of whom the novel was written declined the interview" (or rephrase).

**C) The bridge that crosses the canal is closed for repairs.**

Restrictive "that" correctly defines the bridge that crosses the canal. No commas appear because the clause picks out which bridge. The relative is the subject of "crosses," and the grammar is clean.

So the statement holds: defining "that" correctly identifies the bridge.

**D) Guests which arrive early may wait in the lobby.**

Guests are people, so "which" is the wrong pronoun. Defining people-clauses need "who" or "that." "Which" for human heads is a strong marking red flag.

So the statement is false: repair to "Guests who/that arrive early may wait in the lobby."

**E) The trainer whose tips improved my serve will join practice.**

"Whose tips" correctly shows possession: the tips belong to the trainer. "Whose + noun" is the clean possessive relative pattern for people (and things). The defining clause needs no commas.

So the statement holds: "whose" correctly marks the trainer's tips.
tasks.solution_overview:
People versus things and preposition + whom are the main decisions: an email, an author, a bridge, guests, and a trainer.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Defining "which/that" for things is fine. After a preposition referring to a person, never leave "of who" — raise it to "of whom" (or rephrase). Never use "which" for guests or classmates.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Label each head noun person or thing first. Then check any preposition sitting immediately before the relative. Possessive "whose + noun" earns an easy true when the belonging reading is clear.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The notes, which the lecturer circulated, summarise the chapter.
The applicant whom the panel interviewed withdrew this morning.
Anyone who's still outside should come in before the rain.
The app that tracks sleep was updated overnight.
The room in which the rehearsal takes place is on the second floor.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The notes, which the lecturer circulated, summarise the chapter.**

Non-restrictive "which" correctly adds information about known notes. If you remove the clause, "The notes summarise the chapter" still names a clear noun, so commas + "which" are justified. The relative is the object of "circulated."

So the statement holds: non-restrictive "which" correctly glosses the notes.

**B) The applicant whom the panel interviewed withdrew this morning.**

Object "whom" correctly follows because the panel interviewed the applicant. Swap in "him/her": if that fits, "whom" is justified. The sentence is careful exam English as written.

So the statement holds: object "whom" correctly marks the interviewed applicant.

**C) Anyone who's still outside should come in before the rain.**

"Who's" equals "who is" before "still outside." Expand the contraction in place — "Anyone who is still outside…" — and the sentence still works. Keep the contraction when the expansion fits.

So the statement holds: "who's" expands cleanly to "who is."

**D) The app that tracks sleep was updated overnight.**

Restrictive "that" correctly defines the app that tracks sleep. Everyday tech nouns follow the same who/which/that rules as any other thing. The clause is essential, so there are no commas.

So the statement holds: defining "that" correctly identifies the app.

**E) The room in which the rehearsal takes place is on the second floor.**

"In which" is the formal relative after a preposition for a place: the rehearsal takes place in the room. Formal writing prefers "in which" over a stranded preposition, though both can be grammatical. The defining clause needs no commas.

**Tip:** Formal place relative → in/at/on which.

So the statement holds: "in which" correctly attaches the preposition to the room.
tasks.solution_overview:
These mid-level models cover non-restrictive "which," object "whom," a genuine "who's," defining "that," and formal "in which."

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

If removing the clause still leaves a clear noun, commas + "which" are right for things. Object "whom" follows when you can swap in him/her. Formal place relatives often prefer "in which" over a stranded preposition.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Expand "who's" once — if "who is" fits, keep it. Treat ordinary tech nouns like any other thing for defining "that." Mark true when person/thing, comma pattern, and role inside the clause all agree.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The tent, that leaks in heavy rain, stays in the shed.
The clerk to who complaints should be sent sits at desk four.
Jars whose lids lack labels must be checked before use.
The witness who the lawyer called seemed unsure.
The recipe on which the cake depends needs soft butter.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The tent, that leaks in heavy rain, stays in the shed.**

Commas mark a non-restrictive clause that adds extra detail about a known tent. Everyday nouns still obey the comma rule: non-restrictive wants "which," not "that." Swap the pronoun and keep the commas.

**Trap:** Comma + "that" for a household noun is still an exam near-miss.

So the statement is false: repair to "The tent, which leaks in heavy rain, stays in the shed."

**B) The clerk to who complaints should be sent sits at desk four.**

After "to," the person-relative must be "whom," not "who." Complaints should be sent to the clerk, so the preposition governs an object form. Raise "to who" to "to whom."

**Trap:** Preposition + "who" for people is almost always wrong; exams expect "whom."

So the statement is false: repair to "The clerk to whom complaints should be sent sits at desk four."

**C) Jars whose lids lack labels must be checked before use.**

"Whose" correctly marks possession for jars and lids: jars whose lids lack labels. "Whose" is fine for inanimate nouns in careful English, not only for people. The defining clause needs no commas.

So the statement holds: "whose" correctly marks the jars' lids.

**D) The witness who the lawyer called seemed unsure.**

Object "who" is acceptable in modern usage for the person the lawyer called. Formal style may prefer "whom," but bare "who" as object — with no preposition before it — is rarely marked wrong. The clause is defining and needs no commas.

**Tip:** Bare object "who" is usually fine; a preposition before the relative forces "whom."

So the statement holds: bare object "who" is acceptable without a preceding preposition.

**E) The recipe on which the cake depends needs soft butter.**

"On which" correctly attaches the preposition to a thing: the cake depends on the recipe. Keep preposition + "which" together in formal answers. The defining clause needs no commas.

So the statement holds: "on which" correctly marks dependence on the recipe.
tasks.solution_overview:
Comma + "that," "to who," possession for jars, bare object "who," and formal "on which" are the five checks.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Everyday nouns still obey the comma rule — non-restrictive wants "which." Preposition + who is almost always wrong; raise it to "whom." "Whose" is fine for inanimate lids in careful English.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Fix person-preposition forms first, then comma + that errors. Accept bare object "who" in modern usage when no preposition sits before it, and reward formal "on which" when you see it intact.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The teammates with who we share a pitch signed the same form.
Edinburgh, which remains our favourite base, hosts the fringe each August.
The folder that Mia flagged contains old photos.
A classmate who's been seconded to the drama club still joins practice.
The prototype, which the lab tested last night, failed the heat check.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The teammates with who we share a pitch signed the same form.**

Any preposition before a person-relative wants "whom," so "with who" is wrong. We share a pitch with the teammates; the object form is required. Raise "who" to "whom" after "with."

**Trap:** with/to/for/by + person → "whom" is a reliable mid-level check.

So the statement is false: repair to "The teammates with whom we share a pitch signed the same form."

**B) Edinburgh, which remains our favourite base, hosts the fringe each August.**

Non-restrictive "which" correctly adds a known fact about Edinburgh. City names with commas take "which," not "that" or "who," because the place is already identified by name. The clause is extra detail, not a restricted picker.

So the statement holds: named city + commas correctly take "which."

**C) The folder that Mia flagged contains old photos.**

Defining "that" correctly restricts which folder Mia flagged. Ordinary nouns follow ordinary relative rules, and the clause is essential, so no commas appear. The relative is the object of "flagged."

So the statement holds: restrictive "that" cleanly defines the folder.

**D) A classmate who's been seconded to the drama club still joins practice.**
